en: Preface to the *Biographies of the Eighteen Eminent Worthies of Donglin*:
Formerly, while I was serving as the magistrate of Zhongling, I once passed by the Tiger Creek Bridge at Donglin Temple, the site of Huiyuan’s White Lotus Society.

Seeing it had become a place for the bustling traffic of officials and couriers—reduced to the state of a mere servant for cattle and horses—I could not help but feel deep regret. Now, more than ten years have passed, and I have finally obtained the *Donglin Shi*... [text fragment].
I read the *Biographies of the Eight Noble Sages*. All these gentlemen treated wealth and honor as mere dung and soil, and found their nourishment in the springs and rocks;

their minds transcended the realms of purity and defilement, while their environments reached the excellence of the human and celestial worlds. This causes one’s pulse to throb with emotion and the heart to be stirred, yet there is no way to approach and follow them.

How much more so when one is personally received and guided by them, achieving a wondrous resonance through mutual reliance—need it be said that this need not wait for entry into the Pure Land to attain ultimate bliss, nor for ascending the lotus throne?
How inspiring! This inscription by Fu was carved at Mount Lu, yet it had not yet been widely circulated.

The Venerable Lèyú planned a new undertaking at Qixian Mountain, and subsequently, it was published through woodblock printing at the Vaiśravaṇa Hall in Wumen. I therefore rejoice and write this preface for it.
If one were to cause others to believe this transmission, everyone would see Master Yuan, and everyone would understand Mount Lu.
I suggest that the Master should further seek out the "Portrait of the Eighteen Worthies of Longmen" to append to it, so that it may be transmitted for a thousand generations.
Why envy the *Lanting* or the *Wangchuan* collections? In the past, Zong Shaowen said to Prince Hengyang: "Wealth is like autumn grass; once the season passes, it withers."
I ask those who study the Way: Does this single white lotus flower rot and decay?
No. Written by Huang Ruheng, a resident of Wulin, as the table of contents for the *Biographies of the Eighteen Eminent Men of Donglin*.
Preface by the Dharma Masters Huiyuan, Huiying, Huichi,
Daosheng, Tanshun, Sengrui, Tanheng, and Daobing.
Dharma Master Tanshen, Dharma Master Daojing, Venerable Buddhayaśas,
Venerable Buddhabhadra, Liu Chengzhi, Zhang Ye, Zhou Xuzhi, and Zhang Quan.
The Biographies of One Hundred and Twenty-three Persons, including Zong Bing and Lei Cizong,
Who Did Not Enter the Society; Epilogue to the Biographies of the Various Worthies.
The Biographies of the Eighteen Eminent Sages of Donglin.
Dharma Master Huiyuan.
His secular surname was Jia; he was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. From childhood, he was fond of learning. At the age of thirteen, he followed...
His maternal uncle, surnamed Liu, traveled to study in the regions of Xu and Luo. He was extensively versed in the Six Classics and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*.

Among the veteran scholars and eminent men of his time, none failed to admire his profound insights. At the age of twenty-one, he intended to cross the Yangtze River to study under Fan Ning, but just then Shi Hu died suddenly, leaving the southern route blocked.
His ambition remained unfulfilled; at that time, the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an had established a monastery on Mount Taihang.

At Changshan, he paid his utmost respect [to Daoan], regarding him as his true teacher. Upon first hearing Master An lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained a sudden and profound awakening.
He sighed and said, "The divergent theories of the Nine Schools are all nothing more than chaff. Thereupon, together with his younger brother Huichi, he cast aside his hairpin to receive instruction.
He applied himself to contemplation and recitation with such intensity that night followed day. Consequently, he requested a direct path to the Dharma hall from the śramaṇa Tantan.
Wang Yi provided him with funds for lamps and candles every time. When Master Dao’an heard of this, he remarked, “The Daoist truly knows people.

This master’s spiritual intelligence is extraordinary and transcendent; his will is in profound accord with the ultimate principle. By the age of twenty-four, he was exceptionally skilled at lecturing and exegesis.

Once, when a guest heard his exposition on the meaning of *tathatā* (the true nature of reality) and engaged in a series of challenging questions and debates, his doubts and confusion increased all the more. The master then cited the teachings of Zhuangzi to provide analogies and comparisons.
Those who were deluded felt relieved. Master Dao’an consequently granted permission for him not to abandon the non-Buddhist classics.

Whenever presiding over the assembly, he would often sigh, saying, "He who shall cause the Way to flow to the Eastern lands—will it be Huiyuan? Later, he followed Master Dao’an on a southern journey to Xiangyang.

Encountering the incursions of the Qin general Fu Pi, the disciples were divided and each followed their own path. As they parted at the crossroads, those of venerable virtue all received his instruction and benefit.
The Master alone did not hear a single word. He immediately knelt and requested, saying, "If I am not granted instruction, I fear I shall no longer be human.
An-shi said, "For one such as you, what further cause for concern is there? Thereupon, the Master set out southward with several dozen disciples toward Jingzhou.
While residing at Shangming Temple, he recalled his former association with his dharma-brother Huiyong and made an agreement to build a cottage on Mount Luofu.

In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era (during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty), he arrived at Xunyang and saw that the space between the peaks of Mount Lu was vast and open, a place where one could set the mind at rest. He then established a vihāra there;

however, as the water was still some distance away, he struck the ground with his staff and said, "If this site is fit for habitation, may a spring gush forth from this parched soil. As soon as he spoke, [water appeared].
When clear water suddenly gushed forth, Yangzhou was suffering from a severe drought. The Master went to the side of the pond and recited the *Sūtra of the Dragon King of the Ocean*.

Suddenly, a divine serpent emerged from the pond, and in a short while, there was heavy rain; at the end of the year, the harvest was bountiful. Consequently, it was named Longquan Jingśe (Dragon Spring Monastery).

Master Huiyong previously resided at Xilin on Mount Lu. He wished to invite [Huiyuan] to live together with him, but as Huiyuan’s disciples were already numerous, Huiyong said to the Regional Inspector, Huan Yi:
"Master Yuan is currently flourishing in the propagation of the Way, whereas the dwelling place of this poor monk is cramped and unfit for habitation.
That night, the Master dreamed that a mountain deity told him: "This mountain is sufficient for the spirit to dwell; I pray you do not go elsewhere. That very evening...

A great rain fell with thunderous peals. At dawn the following day, the foot of the mountain had been cleared wide; white sand was spread across the ground, and beams of *pien*, *nan*, and *wen-tzu* wood were strewn everywhere, their origin unknown.
Deeply moved by this great reverence, he established a monastery there, naming its main hall "Divinely Transported" (*Shenyun*).
Because it lay to the east of Master Yong’s hermitage, it was called Donglin (East Forest). This was the eleventh year of the Dàyuán era. This mountain—

Its nine tiers of peaks rise steeply, towering so high as to be cut off from the heavens; yet its dwellings enjoy the full beauty of forests and ravines. It bears Mount Luofeng on its back and is girt by waterfalls on its flanks;

clear streams encircle its steps and white clouds arise from its rafters. (The *Record of Mount Lu* states that Master Kuang Yu, during the transition between the Yin and Zhou dynasties, received the Way from an immortal and established a hall within a cliff;

people called it "the Hermit’s Abode," hence the name Mount Lu. The *Record of Xunyang* notes that the mountain is 3,360 zhang high and 250 li in circumference, with nine tiers and nine branches of water. [From the Prefecture Gazetteer.]

He established a meditation hall on the ninth layer of the mountain’s ridges, a place that enshrined traces of the immortals and was most secluded and profound; all who visited it found their spirits clarified and their demeanors solemnized.
Having heard that the Buddha’s shadow in India was a miraculous manifestation from when the Buddha formerly converted a venomous dragon, he felt a deep sense of joy and inspiration.

Later, after a master of the Vinaya named Xieshe described the radiant appearance of the image, he constructed a grotto-dwelling facing the mountain and overlooking a stream, painting it in muted colors.
It was depicted so that from afar it appeared like mist and clouds. Furthermore, five inscriptions were composed and engraved upon stone. These were by Meng Huaiyu, Governor of Jiangzhou;
Wang Qiao, Vice Governor; Zhang Ye, Attendant-in-Ordinary; Yin Yin, Governor of Jin’an; and Mao Xiuzhi, Gentleman of the Palace Gate.
The Secretary-General Yin Wei, the Military Aide Wang Mu, the Filial and Upright Fan Yuezhi, the recluse Zong Bing, and others all composed eulogies and inscriptions (found in the *Lushan ji*).
Previously, when Tao Kan of Xunyang was serving as Governor of Guangzhou, fishermen saw a divine light in the sea;
they cast their nets and caught a golden image of Mañjuśrī. An inscription stated that it had been fashioned by King Aśoka. Later, merchants...
In Haidong, a single halo was obtained; it was used to restore the image, fitting it as if by sewing. Zhi Kan sent it to the presiding monk of Hanxi Temple in Wuchang.
The monk Sengzhen frequently traveled to Xiakou; one night he dreamed that the temple was on fire, yet the chamber of this image alone was protected by a divine power.

He hurried back to the temple, and indeed it had burned down, while the image chamber remained intact. When Zhi Kan was overseeing Jiangzhou, he welcomed the image and was about to bring it back when they reached—

While crossing by boat, he drowned. The people of Jing and Chu sang this ballad: "Tao was truly a hero of the sword; his image is marked by divine spirit. Soaring like clouds, yet dwelling in the mud—how vast and far apart!
It can be reached through the utmost sincerity, but it is difficult to summon by mere force. When the temple was completed, the Master arrived at the riverbank.
He prayed with great devotion, and the image suddenly emerged from its concealment. He then welcomed it to the Shen-yun Hall and constructed a multi-storied pavilion to enshrine it.

Consequently, he composed the "Eulogy on the Auspicious Image of Mañjuśrī. He once remarked that while the names of samādhis in the various teachings are exceedingly numerous, this one is of high merit and easy to advance toward.

They took the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) as their primary focus. Soon thereafter, practitioners who were diligent in the precepts and tranquil in mind, as well as lay devotees who had severed ties with the mundane world, arrived without prior appointment.

These included Huiyong (who, like Master An, had previously resided at Xilin), Huichi (the younger brother of Master Yuan by the same mother), Daosheng and Tanshun (both disciples of Kumārajīva), Sengrui, Tanheng, Daobing, Tanzhen, and Daojing (all disciples of Master Yuan), and Buddhayaśas (translated as Jue-ming).

Buddhabhadra (a native of Kaśmīra). The eminent scholar Liu Chengzhi (styled Yimin), along with Zhang Ye, Zhou Xuzhi, Zhang Quan, Zong Bing, Lei Cizong, and others, formed a society to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; they were known in the world as the "Eighteen Worthies.

Furthermore, leading a group of one hundred and twenty-three people, they collectively cultivated the practices for the Pure Land and constructed [an image of] Amitābha Buddha of the Western Paradise.

A sacred image was established, and a vegetarian fast was held with a formal vow. Liu Yimin was commissioned to compose a "Text of Vows," while Wang Qiao and others further composed "Poems on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection" to manifest their resolve.
The Master’s countenance was solemn and majestic; those who gazed upon him felt their hearts tremble with awe.
There was a śramaṇa who arrived carrying a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) as an offering; not daring to present it, he secretly left it at the edge of the master’s seat and departed.

The Dharma Master Huiyi, being upright and possessing little tolerance for pretense, said to his disciple Huibao: "You gentlemen are superficial, which is why you all admire and submit to Master Yuan’s reputation from afar.
Whenever we go to the mountain and encounter the Master lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, whenever I wish to pose a challenge, my heart immediately trembles with fear."
He broke into a sweat. Huchi said to Huibao, "This gentleman’s speech and demeanor are truly worthy of respect and submission.

When Yin Zhongkan was serving as the Governor of Jingzhou, he entered the mountains to pay his respects to the Master. Together they stood beneath a pine tree by a northern stream and discussed the Way of the *I Ching* until sunset, forgetting all fatigue.
Zhongkan sighed and said, "The Master’s wisdom and insight are profound and clear; it is truly difficult for others to equal them. The Master also said, "As for your own talent..."

[He] distinguished [himself]. A spring such as this flowed forth (later people named the place "Cleverness and Wisdom Spring"). Wang Mi, the Minister of Education, and Wang Mo, the Commander of the Guard, both admired his character and virtue;
they paid their respects from afar (there was a correspondence of letters between them). When Lu Xun occupied Jiangzhou, he entered the mountains to visit the Master.
The Master had been a fellow student with Xun’s father, Xia, in his youth; upon seeing Xun, he joyfully reminisced about their past. His disciples remonstrated with him, saying:
Hui-xun became a rebel against the state; could he not have been suspected by others? The Master said, "In our Buddhist Dharma, the mind has no grasping or rejecting.

Those who understand will naturally perceive this. Why should this be feared? When Emperor Wu of Song advanced to suppress Hui-xun and set up his headquarters at Sangwei, his attendants said, "Master Huiyuan has long been the sovereign of Mount Lu and was on very intimate terms with Hui-xun.
Emperor Wu of Song replied, "Master Huiyuan stands beyond the mundane world."
"How could one doubt this? he thought. He then dispatched a messenger with a letter and gifts of money and silk.
There was a practitioner who came to serve the Master; he was skilled at driving away snakes, and the snakes were completely cleared away. Consequently, he was called the "Snake-Driving Practitioner.

A tiger used to come and go, frequently seen following his tracks, yet it never harmed anyone. People called it the "Mountain-Wandering Tiger. The Master and the members of the community would often go to the Shangfang (Upper Hall) for recreation and rest.
At the summit of the peak, he suffered from the distance to water. One day, a tiger pawed at the rock, and water gushed forth from it; consequently, it was named Tiger-Pawed Spring (Hupao Quan).
Furthermore, on another peak, he composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and for this reason, the peak was named Thrown-Pen Peak (Zhibi Feng).

Initially, as the Great Teaching spread, the scriptural volumes were incomplete in Jiangdong, the methods of Chan were unheard of, and the Vinaya-piṭaka was largely deficient. The Master then commanded his disciples...
Fajing, Faling, and others traveled far beyond the Pamir Mountains and returned after many years, all of whom obtained Sanskrit manuscripts.
Formerly, when Master An was in Guanzhong, he invited Dharmanandi to translate the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; however, this man was not yet proficient in the Jin language.
There were many points of doubt and stagnation. Later, when Saṃghadeva arrived, [Dao'an] immediately requested that he retranslate [the *Dharmapada-śāstra*] along with the *Tri-dharmaka-śāstra*.
Thereupon, these two treatises flourished. The Master then composed a preface to bequeath to students. He heard that Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong.
He sent a letter to establish friendly relations. Kumārajīva replied in his letter, saying: "I have received your gracious gift and have gained a rough understanding of your reputation and virtue.
The Sūtras state that in the final age, there shall be a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma in the East. How admirable it is that you, O Benevolent One, so skillfully propagate the Way!

When Dharmaruci entered the territory of Qin, my teacher dispatched his disciple Tanyong to invite him to Guanzhong, where he translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* for circulation throughout the Jin state. To the West...
The monks of the land all proclaimed that there were Mahāyāna bodhisattvas in the land of Han, and they regularly turned toward the east to pay homage and offer their hearts to Mount Lu.
When Buddhabhadra arrived, the Master immediately requested that he bring out various sūtras on dhyāna and saṃkhyā.

Thereupon, the scriptures on dhyāna and precepts emerged from Mount Lu, numbering nearly one hundred fascicles. Previously, this land had never possessed the teaching of the eternal permanence of *nirvāṇa*.
[He] spoke only of the longevity of his life span. The Master said, "The Buddha is the ultimate. That which is ultimate is without change.

How could the principle of non-change ever come to an end? Thereupon, he composed the *Treatise on the Dharma-nature* (*Faxing lun*) in fourteen chapters. When Kumārajīva saw it, he sighed in admiration, saying:
In the border regions, the sutras had not yet been seen; thus, [the Master’s teachings] were in dark accord with reason.

The Ruler of Qin, admiring his reputation, commissioned a new translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and sent a letter requesting a preface. Because the text was voluminous and extensive, the Master abridged its essentials into twenty fascicles and composed a preface for it (the *Prajñā-śāstra* translated by Kumārajīva originally consisted of one hundred fascicles).
When Huan Xuan campaigned against Yin Zhongkan, he summoned the Master to cross Tiger Brook, but the Master feigned illness.
He did not go. When Huiyuan was about to enter the mountains, his attendants said, "In the past, Yin Zhongkan paid his respects to Huiyuan;

we beg you, sir, not to humble yourself. Huiyuan replied, "Zhongkan is but a dead man. When Huiyuan saw the Master, he involuntarily knelt, and the questions and difficulties he had harbored [were resolved].
He did not dare to speak further. When the conversation turned to military expeditions, the Master simply did not answer.

Later, when Huan [Xuan]—who possessed a majesty that rivaled the sovereign—urged him to take office, the Master responded with firm resolve. Huan was unable to force his will upon him. Subsequently, Huan sought to purge and eliminate the monastic community.

He issued an edict to his subordinates, saying: "Among the ranks of śramaṇas, only those who can expound the scriptures and whose conduct is disciplined and refined may be entrusted with propagating the Great Transformation.
Any who violate these standards shall be dismissed from office. The only exception is Mount Lu, the abode of those possessing the Way and virtue;
it shall not be subject to this investigation. The Master (Huiyuan) consequently sent a letter establishing detailed regulations, all of which Xuan fully understood.

He followed this course. Initially, when Xie Bing assisted in governance, he maintained that śramaṇas should pay homage to the king. He Chong submitted a memorial stating that this was contrary to ritual propriety.
When Daoyuan was at Gushu, he again reiterated Bing’s argument. The Master replied in a letter, saying: "The kāṣāya is not a garment for attending the imperial court."
The alms bowl is not a vessel for the corridors of the imperial court. A guest from beyond the mundane world ought not to pay homage to a sovereign;

thus, he composed the "Five Treatises on the Śramaṇa Not Paying Homage to the Sovereign. The first clarifies that those remaining at home possess natural affection for their kin and observe the rites of serving their lord.

The second clarifies that those who have left the household seek to realize their aspirations and transform their worldly ways to attain the Way; how could they be treated the same as those following secular codes?

Regarding their ritual veneration: the Three Illuminations (trividyā) seek the ultimate principle (*zong*) rather than conforming to transformation. "Ultimate principle" refers to *nirvāṇa* (translated as "neither arising nor ceasing"), which is unchanging.
They take the exhaustion of transformation as their abode. Those who do not conform to transformation hold that birth may be extinguished and the spirit may enter stillness;

this state of the spirit’s stillness and the severance of the realm is called *nirvāṇa*. Thus, they do not follow along with the continuous arising and transforming of birth, nor with the infinite flux of conditioned phenomena.
This is why they do not serve kings or lords, holding their own principles in high esteem; how could they ever perform acts of ritual veneration?

It is said that those who embody the ultimate reality (tǐjí) do not engage in dualistic response; that is, the sovereigns of successive dynasties who embodied the ultimate reality were concerned solely with the affairs within the four quarters [of the realm].
Yet they cannot both be governed simultaneously from beyond the mundane realm; therefore, it is said that [the worldly teachings] do not respond universally.
The Way of Heaven and Earth exhausts its efficacy in the process of transformation and evolution; the virtue of the sovereign reaches its ultimate in accordance with and penetration of principle.

Compared to the uniquely transcendent teaching and the immutable source [of Buddhism], their relative superiority and inferiority are clear. As for the Way of the Tathāgata, there is nothing to which it does not respond. Its five branches of knowledge manifest...
"The spirit is exhausted but does not perish. This means that just as fire is transmitted from one piece of wood to another, so too is the spirit transmitted from one form to another.
As fire passes to different pieces of wood, so does the spirit pass to different forms. Birth and death occur simultaneously; their coming and going are without end.

Those who attain clear awakening return to the root, while those deluded by principle pursue external objects. After a short while, Xuán usurped the throne and immediately issued an edict stating: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and grandiose..."

I have not yet fully understood this. Previously, out of deference to my master, I caused you to arouse feelings of reverence; now that the matter rests with me, I ought to exercise the utmost humility.

Therefore, O practitioners of the Way, do not offer salutations again. When Huan Xuan fled westward and Emperor An returned from Jiangling to the capital, He Wuji, the Protector of the State, urged the Master to go out to welcome him.
The Master cited illness as an excuse and did not go. The Emperor then dispatched an envoy...
He inquired after his well-being. The Master submitted a memorial declining on account of illness, and the Emperor again issued an edict to console and respond to him.

The Master once lectured on the *Sangfu jing* (likely referring to the *Xiaji*, *Daji*, and *Sizhi* chapters of the *Liji*). Lei Cizong, Zong Bing, and others all held the scrolls and received his instructions.

Later, when Cizong composed a commentary (*yishu*), he headed it with the title "The Lei Family. Zong Bing sent him a letter reproaching him, saying: "In the past, we received this face-to-face from you..."

Regarding the Master Shi: why is he now called by the surname Lei? (Lu Deming’s *Phonetic Commentary on the Mao Shih* states that Zhou Xuzhi and Lei Cizong both received the meaning of the Odes from Dharma Master Yuan;
this is also of this same category). Shi Huiyao was troubled by the lack of a water clock (*ke-lou*) in the mountains. He therefore erected a twelve-petaled lotus flower upon the water;
as it rotated with the waves, it divided and determined day and night to serve as the intervals for his practice of the Way. This was called the "Lotus" [clock].

Liu Le was skilled in calligraphy and composition. Once, while at Mount Shan, he climbed a pine tree and let out a long whistle; a gentle breeze gathered from afar and the birds cried out in lamentation.
He felt a sense of transcendent self-satisfaction. Later, he consulted his teacher, saying, "The monastic discipline prohibits pipes, strings, singing, and dancing."
"If one were to sing or laugh, would that be permissible? The Master said, "If it is done with a distracted mind, all such acts are contrary to the Dharma.
Zhe simply bowed and withdrew. The Master resided in the mountains for thirty years, never entering the secular world. He devoted himself solely to the diligent recitation of the Pure Land.

For the first eleven years, he concentrated his mind and focused his thoughts; three times he beheld the sacred countenance, yet he remained grave and spoke not of it. Thereafter, for nineteen [years]...

On the evening of the last day of the seventh month, while rising from meditative concentration in the eastern niche of the Prajñā Terrace, he beheld Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void of space.
Within the halo of light were various transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing as attendants on either side.
He further saw flowing waters and radiant light divided into fourteen branches, streaming upward and downward, proclaiming the teachings of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
There was the sound of the "Eternal Non-Self. The Buddha told him, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you.

Seven days from now, you shall be born in my land. He also saw Buddhasiṃha, Huichi (who passed away in the eighth year of Yixi), Huiming (who passed away in the tenth year of Yixi), and Liu Yimin (who passed away in the sixth year of Yixi) standing by the Buddha’s side. They came forward and bowed to the Master, saying, "The Master's aspiration lies in..."
"Why have you arrived so late? The Master said to Fa-jing and Hui-bao, "In the eleven years since I first resided here, I have seen the marks of the Buddha three times;
now I see them again. It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. He further said, "The seven-day period has arrived."
This was a gradual process. He then fell ill and composed his final testament, saying: "In my past years, when I had come to understand the nature of destiny, I took up my practice on this mountain.
Having personally discerned that my time must surely come to an end, I wished to sever all external ties in order to pursue my aspirations.

However, because my nature is weak in making firm resolutions, I allowed those of similar inclination to draw me in; thus, the excessive affection of the worthy of the time moved my heart through the resonance of kindred spirits."

I perceive that my physical form and its movements are in decline; this year I have already reached the age of eighty-three. Looking up, I reflect upon your instructions regarding our separation; looking down, I lament my own sense of failure.
I have allowed this life to pass away in vain, grieving for the depth of my past illnesses.

Now, at this final hour, I shall expose my remains beneath the pine forest and use the mountain ridge itself as a tomb, without the use of earth or wood to construct it. This is the way of the ancients...

I pray that you will not violate these rites. If the divine principle is not obscure, I hope that my sincerity may reach him. The World-Honored One of Great Compassion shall surely assist me through the Way.
His disciples wailed and lamented as if they had lost their own parents; yet, because the master’s worldly ties were difficult to sever, he established a seven-day period for the expression of grief.
When the time arrived, he finally entered into quiescence, which was on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era.
The disciples could not bear to leave the corpse exposed; together with Ruan Kan, the Governor of Xunyang, they enshrined the entire body and buried it on the Western Ridge.
They piled stones to form a stupa. Xie Lingyun erected a stele to commemorate his virtues, and Zhang Ye composed a preface, styling himself a "disciple.
Zong Bing further erected a stele at the temple gate to manifest the master’s virtuous achievements. As the Master was about to pass away, the venerable elders requested that he—

He used fermented soybean wine to treat his illness. The Master said, "The Vinaya contains no such textual precedent; I request that you drink rice gruel. The Master replied, "The sun has already passed its zenith.
He then requested honey mixed with water. [Huiyuan] then ordered him to open the Vinaya and search for the relevant text; he died before the scroll was even half-finished.
His collected works—including various prefaces, inscriptions, eulogies, poems, and records—total ten scrolls, titled the *Lushan ji* (carved in woodblocks at Yuefu). From the Buddha...
It is said that Tuche, Daoshi, Master Yuan, Dharma Master Tanshun, and Sengrui served as National Preceptors for five generations.
In the second year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously titled Great Master Bianjue.

In the third year of the Shengyuan era (the fourth year of the Tianfu era of Emperor Gaozu of the Jin dynasty, corresponding to the Southern Tang ruler Li Yu), he was posthumously titled Zhengjue. In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era of Emperor Taizong of the Great Song, he was posthumously titled...
The Stupa of Master Yuanwu’s Serene Stillness.
Dharma Master Huiyong and Dharma Master Xilin.
Huiyong was of the Pan clan of Henei; he left home at the age of twelve and served the śramaṇa Zhu Tantan.
In the present, he first practiced meditation at Mount Heng, where he and Master Huiyuan both relied upon Dharma Master Daoan. They planned to build a monastery on Mount Luofu;
however, as Master Huiyuan was detained by Master Daoan, the Master intended to cross the Five Ridges first.

At the beginning of the Taiyuan era, he arrived at Xunyang, where Tao Fan, the Regional Inspector, had long admired his spiritual influence and invited him to stay and rest at Mount Lu. Fan donated his residence to be converted into Xilin Monastery.

He served his teacher, wearing simple robes and eating coarse vegetables. He cultivated his mind with diligence and self-restraint; his countenance was always smiling, and his speech never harmed others.

At the summit of the peak, he built a separate thatched hut where he dwelt in meditative contemplation. Those who entered his room would constantly perceive a wondrous fragrance, and for this reason, it was called "Fragrant Valley" (Xianggu).
A tiger lived with him; whenever anyone approached, it would immediately drive them away. When Master Huiyuan arrived at Longquan, Huan Yi established Donglin Temple for him.
For thirty years, his shadow never left the mountain. Master [Hui]yi resided at Xilin, where he behaved in the same manner.

Once, while returning from a local town on his way back to the mountain at dusk, the village head of Wuqiao was riding a horse under the influence of alcohol; he blocked the path across the road and refused to let the Master pass.
The Master pointed at the horse with his staff; the horse bolted in alarm, and the camp commander fell to the ground. The Master comforted him and they returned together.
The commander fell ill and went to the monastery to confess his transgressions. The Master said, "This was not my intention," and he performed prayers on his behalf. He recovered shortly thereafter.

When He Wujī, General of the South, was stationed at Xunyang, he reached Hu Xi and invited Master Huiyuan and the Master [Huiyue]. Huiyuan possessed great renown and prestige, and thus followed along.
He was accompanied by over a hundred followers; his speech was lofty and his discourse elegant, and his deportment was worthy of admiration.

The Master arrived with a flowing grace beneath the pines, wearing a hempen robe that reached only halfway down his calves, carrying a mendicant’s staff and holding an alms bowl. Huiwuji said to the assembly, "Master Yong’s style of pure detachment exceeds even that of Master Huiyuan.

The Master set his sincerity as his standard and planted his vows for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). In the tenth year of the Yixi era, while he was ill, he suddenly withdrew [from the world].

As he was seeking his robes and wishing to rise, the assembly asked him in alarm, "Master," and he replied, "The Buddha has come. His words ended, and he passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for seven days before it finally dissipated.

He was buried to the southwest of the monastery at the age of eighty-three. During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial decree was issued to rebuild the stupa and pavilion, and he was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Jueji (Awakened Quiescence) and the stupa was named Shizhi (True Wisdom).
Dharma Master Huichi was the half-brother of Master Huiyuan. From childhood, he memorized as much in a single day as others would in ten days.

At the age of eighteen, he entered the service of Master Dao’an alongside his elder brother, where he studied the various sutras extensively and attained mastery over the Tripiṭaka. When [Master Dao’an]...
While the Duke was in Xiangyang, he dispatched Master Huiyuan to travel eastward. The Master subsequently settled at Mount Lu.
He stood eight chi tall, and his patched robe reached down to his knees; he had three hundred disciples, of whom he was the preeminent leader.

Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang, invited the Master to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, drawing crowds from all quarters like clouds. Wang Xun of Langya wrote a letter to Fan Ning [concerning this].
He asked which of the two, Huiyuan or Daochi, was superior. Ning replied, "I truly consider them both to be 'worthy elder brothers' and 'worthy younger brothers.

Sengxun wrote back in reply: "If one were merely to be like a younger brother, such a thing has truly never existed; how much less could they be considered 'worthy'? Kumārajīva, while in Guanzhong, held them both in high esteem from afar.
He frequently sent letters to maintain friendly relations. In the third year of the Long’an era, he took leave of his elder brother to enter Shu.

Master Huiyuan detained him, saying, "In human life, people cherish gathering together; you alone delight in separation. The Master replied, "Those who harbor lingering attachments to gathering should not have left the household life in the first place.
Now that I have severed my desires to seek the Way, I am simply taking the Western Land as my destination. He then departed with a heavy heart and arrived at [Pei] in Chengdu.
Xian resided at Longyuan Temple and propagated the Buddha-dharma extensively. Those who ascended his hall were said to have "climbed the Dragon Gate.

In the eighth year of the Yixi era, he passed away at the age of seventy-six. At the time of his death, he left a final instruction: "Diligently observe the monastic precepts and devote yourself single-mindedly to pure practice."
He entrusted the scriptures of the eastern chamber to Daohong and the Vinaya texts of the western chamber to Tanlan.
Because Daohong’s conduct was pure and his faculties sharp, and Tanlan’s spiritual insight was divinely inspired, both were able to follow in the footsteps of their master.

Dharma Master Daosheng was a native of Julu during the Wei dynasty. In his youth, he followed Zhu Fatai to leave the household life; upon encountering the scriptures and proclamations, he could recite them after a single reading.

While still at the age of *zhixue* (the age of formal study), he ascended the lecture seat; his exposition was lucid and discerning, such that even those of long-standing reputation could not surpass him.
I venture to respond to this challenge. Initially, he relied upon Mount Lu, always regarding wisdom and understanding as the foundation for entering the Way.
He then traveled to Chang’an with Sengrui, Huiyan, Huiguan, and others to study under Kumārajīva in the Guanzhong region.

All his fellow monks looked up to his divine intuition. Once, he sighed deeply and said: "Since the arrival of the scriptures in the East, translators have repeatedly obstructed them, causing many points of provisional teaching to remain stagnant."
[The text] states: Wen was not yet fully proficient in the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Only when one forgets the trap to catch the fish can one begin to discourse upon the Way.

Thereupon, Wen scrutinized the ultimate and conventional truths (*zhen-su*), refined his understanding of emptiness and existence (*kong-you*), and investigated cause and effect. He then established the doctrines that "goodness does not entail retribution" and "sudden enlightenment leads to Buddhahood.

Furthermore, he authored the *Treatise on the Two Truths* (*Er-di lun*), the *Treatise on the Ever-Abiding Buddha-nature* (*Fo-xing chang-you lun*), and the *Treatise on the Buddha Having No Pure Land* (*Fo wu jing-tu lun*). [He also composed] the *Yingyou yuan...* [text fragment].
The treatise comprehensively encompasses the profound and subtle principles of the ancient teachings. Among those who cling to the literal text, resentment and jealousy arose in competition.
Furthermore, the Master [Tanyan] noted that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Faxian had arrived first (in a six-fascicle version).

The sutra states: "With the exception of the icchantikas, all possess Buddha-nature. The Master remarked: "All who receive their physical form from the two polarities of heaven and earth possess the correct cause for nirvana; even the icchantika..."

Among the myriad classes of sentient beings, how could any be uniquely devoid of Buddha-nature? It is simply that the transmission of the sutras has not yet been complete. Thus he proclaimed that even icchantikas can all attain Buddhahood;
at that time, as the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* had not yet been translated, his solitary insight emerged first, causing the established schools of monks to take offense.

He considered this to be contrary to the sūtras and consequently revealed it before the great assembly, whereupon [the opponent] was expelled and sent away. The Master assumed a solemn countenance and made a vow, saying:

"If what I have spoken is contrary to the sūtras, may my body be afflicted with leprosy; if it does not contradict the true nature of reality (bhūtatathatā), I pray that on the day of my passing, [I may attain parinirvāṇa]."
He sat upon the lion throne and then brushed off his robes and departed. Later, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reached the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*), it stated:
"Even though an icchantika has severed all roots of goodness, they still possess Buddha-nature. At this, all the masters were filled with shame and submitted to his authority.

Banished from the capital, the Master returned south and entered Mount Huqiu. There he gathered stones as his disciples and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. When he reached the section concerning the icchantikas, he said:

He proclaimed that there is Buddha-nature and asked, "Does what I have said accord with the Buddha's mind? Whereupon all the rocks nodded their heads. Within ten days, the assembly of students gathered like clouds.
Suddenly, thunder shook the Qingyuan Garden, and a dragon ascended to heaven from the Buddha Hall; consequently, the temple was renamed Longguang (Dragon Light).
At the temple, the Master invited the Kasmiri Vinaya Master to translate the *Śrāmaṇera-śīla-sūtra*, which has been transmitted to the world. This being done—
He then took his leave of the assembly and retired once more to Mount Lu to join the Lotus Society. After a long time, he returned to the capital and resided at Qingxia Temple.
During a great assembly of śramaṇas convened by Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Emperor personally presided over the seating arrangement. When the meal was served, it had been for some time;

the assembly suspected that the hour had passed midday. The Emperor said, "It is only now reaching midday. Daosheng then remarked, "The bright sun adorns the heavens. If the Emperor says it is only now midday, how can it not be midday? Thereupon, he...
He ate using chopsticks. The entire assembly followed his example, and there was none who did not marvel at his quick-witted eloquence.
At that time, King Hong, Fan Tai, and Yan Yanzhi all held him in high esteem for his character and conduct, following him to inquire about the Way.

On the gengzi day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, as he sat upon the dais at Mount Lu to preach the Dharma, the assembly saw his fly-whisk fall to the ground in a flurry; he then leaned back, resting his head upon his armrest.
He manifested a transformation as if entering meditative concentration. When the various masters heard of this, they further believed that his previous vows had received verification.

The following day, he was buried on a western ridge of Mount Lu. Initially, the monk Sengzhao of Guanzhong had begun his commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, and while everyone savored its meaning, the Master further elucidated its profound purport;
people marveled at its subtlety. His writings included commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and the *Kṣudraka-prajñāpāramitā*.

All the various sutras possess commentaries; at that time, because the Master was able to expound upon the meaning of how icchantikas attain Buddhahood, he thereby revealed his treatises on sudden enlightenment and the non-reception of karmic retribution.
Dharma Master Tanshun was a native of Huanglong.

Having left home at a young age, he received instruction from Kumārajīva and expounded upon various scriptures, exhaustively elucidating the subtle principles of form and emptiness and non-attachment.
Kumārajīva marveled, saying, "This youth is a vessel of extraordinary talent. Later, he came to Mount Lu to practice together with [Huiyuan].
Jingye. Ningman Xiaowei Liu Zunxiao established a monastery in Jiangling and invited the Master to initiate its construction. There, he extensively propagated the Way of the Nianfo Samādhi.
In the second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while seated in meditation before the assembly; a rare fragrance filled the room.
He was seventy-nine years of age.

Dharma Master Sengrui was a native of Jizhou. While traveling and studying in various regions, he once journeyed through the western borders of Shu and was plundered by bandits, who forced him to herd sheep.
A merchant found him strange and suspected he was a śramaṇa; when questioned about the meaning of the scriptures, there was nothing he did not know.
Zongda immediately provided gold to redeem him. Later, he traveled through various kingdoms of India and returned to Guanzhong, where he consulted with Kumārajīva on the meaning of the sūtras.
When Kumārajīva was translating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he noted that according to the version by Dharmarakṣa, it says: "Heaven sees man."
When people saw [the deity] Tian, Kumārajīva said, "This statement is merely too literal. Huì said, "Could it not be that humans and devas have met, so that both may see one another?
Kumārajīva was pleased and subsequently adopted those words. After some time, he entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan to cultivate the practice of *śubha-karma* (pure deeds).
Subsequently, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Wuyi Temple, where he lectured on various sutras; his listeners admired and submitted to him. During the Song dynasty, Peng...

King Yikang of the city invited the Preceptor to his palace to receive the precepts. The Preceptor said, "According to the rites, one comes as a student. Thereupon, the King entered the monastery and reverently received the dharma of the precepts.
The King offered a sable fur robe to the Preceptor for his regular use as a seat-cover. The King had secretly purchased it for thirty thousand coins.
The Preceptor said, "Although this is not something suitable for me to wear, it is a gift from the King and cannot be discarded. When the King heard this, he was delighted.
His reverence increased all the more. Xie Lingyun was deeply devoted to Buddhist principles and had mastered many regional dialects and foreign sounds.

He once sought verification from the Master regarding the phonetic readings of characters in the scriptures, whereupon the Master composed the *Xunshi shisi yin* (Explanations of the Fourteen Vowels), through which the Sanskrit and Chinese became clearly illuminated.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he passed away without illness after announcing to the assembly: "I am about to depart. He then faced west, joined his palms, and died.
The assembly saw a golden lotus flower within his chamber suddenly vanish. He was eighty-five years of age.
Dharma Master Tanheng was a native of Hedong.
Having relied upon Master Huiyuan for ordination as a youth, he was only thirteen years old when he was already able to—

In his lectures and expositions on both internal and external classics, there was nothing he did not master. His virtuous conduct was pure and solitary, earning him the profound respect and submission of all.
It was common for herds of deer to wander playfully around the corner of his seat. Since entering Mount Lu, he had devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he sat upright with palms joined and, chanting the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice, passed away at the age of seventy-two.
Dharma Master Daobing: Dharma Master Daobing was a native of Yingchuan. Having joined the monastic order as a youth, he became a disciple of Master Huiyuan.

He was thoroughly versed in the sutras and the vinaya, while also possessing a profound understanding of the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. His character and integrity were solitary and lofty; his words accorded perfectly with his deeds. He devoted himself to the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nienfo sanmei*) until his mind reached its ultimate realization.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Wang Qian, the Governor of Yuzhang, entered the mountains to pay his respects and invited him to serve as the abbot of the mountain to succeed Master Daoyuan.
The assembly, recognizing him as the Dharma heir of Daoyuan, all looked up to him with reverence.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he gathered the community for a session of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and passed away while seated. He was seventy-one years of age.
Dharma Master Tanshen:

Dharma Master Tanshen was a native of Guangling. In his youth, he left the household life under Master Huiyuan. He diligently cultivated the practice of purity while concurrently lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

His commentary on this sūtra circulated throughout the world. He frequently composed the "Treatise on Adversity and Success" (*Qiongtong lun*) to clarify his past cultivation and described the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*).

He recorded these to document his rebirth. Furthermore, he could distinguish the colors of birds and beasts and discern their natures—whether spirited or dull—and he thoroughly understood the flavors of plants and trees, whether their branches were bitter or sweet, exhausting their principles with marvelous precision. People knew that he possessed secret realization.
In the seventeenth year of the Yuanjia era, he gathered the assembly and said, "Since the founding of this temple until now, fifty years have passed. My journey to the West..."
He practiced meditation, always remaining at the very rear. He then sat in the full lotus posture and recited the Buddha’s name one hundred times; he held his breath until it ceased.
He was eighty years of age. As for Dharma Master Daojing:
he was of the Wang clan of Langya. His grandfather, Wang Ningzhi, served as the Governor of Jiangzhou, and Daojing subsequently followed Master Huiyuan to leave the household life.

At the age of seventeen, he was extensively versed in the sutras and śāstras, memorizing ten thousand words daily. He often lamented that it was difficult to maintain the precepts in their entirety throughout one's entire life;
thus, he vowed to purify the six sense faculties by observing only a single precept, regarding this as the essential means for attaining liberation.

Master Huiyuan, recognizing his steadfastness and integrity, permitted him to focus his resolve on the recitation of the Buddha’s name, which he practiced morning and night without ceasing. After Master Huiyuan passed away, he entered Mount Ruoye during the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty.

In the first year [of his tenure], Yuan addressed the assembly, saying, "My former master has given me his command; it is time for me to depart. He then sat upright, chanted the name of the Buddha, and passed away.
The assembly saw a radiance fill the room, which did not dissipate until some time had passed. He was fifty-two years of age.
The Venerable Buddhayaśas (the Jin translation meaning "Awakened Brilliance") was of Brahmin descent from the kingdom of Kaśmīra. A śramaṇa came to his house to beg for food;

his father, who had originally been a non-Buddhist, became enraged and spat upon him. Consequently, [Buddhayaśas] became paralyzed and lame in his hands and feet. A sorcerer said to him, "It is because of..."
He had offended a noble sage; the sage immediately invited this śramaṇa to repent his transgression. Within ten days, he recovered. Consequently, Xieshe was ordained at the age of thirteen.
While traveling through a vast wilderness with his teacher, he encountered a tiger. Xieshe said, "The tiger is already full; it will surely not harm people.
As they proceeded further along the road, they indeed found the remains of a carcass. By the age of fifteen, he could recite ten thousand words of scripture every day. Because...
Because his alms-round (*piṇḍapāta*; in the Jin language, "begging for food") interfered with his studies, he became distressed. An arhat came to take his place in begging for food.
By the age of nineteen, he had recited the scriptures to the extent of several million [verses]. His character was simple and haughty; he was not held in high regard by others.

At thirty, he was still a *śrāmaṇera* (novice), and he further studied the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and worldly arts and techniques under his maternal uncle. (Both Buddhist insiders and non-Buddhist outsiders have the five sciences; the internal five...)

The sciences (*vidyā*) are five: first, grammar; second, medicine; third, incantations; fourth, arts and crafts; and fifth, logic. As for the "five external sciences," the first four are the same as above, while the last one is the science of seals and talismans (*mudrā-vidyā*).

Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kucha, he was received with great honor and hospitality. Shortly thereafter, Kumārajīva arrived, and [Dharmakṣema] proceeded to study the *Abhidharma* treatises and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under him.
When Kumārajīva returned to Kucha with his mother, Dharmakṣema remained behind to spread the teachings. Emperor Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to invade Kucha.

When Kumārajīva was captured, the Master heard the news and said with joy, "Kumārajīva and I have not yet exhausted our mutual aspirations; now that he has suddenly been taken captive, when shall we meet again?
Ten years later, the Master traveled east to Kucha and propagated the Dharma teachings extensively, while Kumārajīva remained in Guzang.

He sent a messenger to entreat him [to stay]. Fearing that the people of the country would stop his journey, the Master took clear water, added medicine to it, and recited several dozen words of incantation.
He then gave it to his disciples to wash their feet. That very night they set out; by dawn they had traveled several hundred li, and the pursuers could not catch up.
He asked his disciples, "What did you perceive? They replied, "We heard only the whistling of a swift wind, and there were tears in our eyes."
The Master further recited mantras over water to wash his feet, and only then did he cease. Upon arriving at Guzang, Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an.
Hearing that King Yao was pressuring him to take concubines and handmaidens, the Master sighed and said, "Kumārajīva is like fine cotton wool; how can one allow him to enter a thorny forest?

Kumārajīva then urged King Yao to dispatch an envoy to welcome the Master. Once he arrived, a separate monastery was established for him within the Xiaoyao Garden, where he was provided with the four requisites.
He maintained himself by receiving nothing at all; when the time came for alms, he would take but a single meal.

At that time, as Kumārajīva translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the masters consulted one another to resolve difficult points until the terminology and principles were finally settled. The Master’s beard was red and he was skilled in explaining the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*;
thus, his contemporaries called him "The Red-bearded Śāstrin. During the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, he translated the forty-four-fascicle *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
[He translated] twenty-two fascicles of sutras. In the eighth year of the Yixi era, he came to Mount Lu to join the community. Later, he took his leave and returned to his native land.
From Jibin, he entrusted one scroll of the *Gaganagañja-sūtra* to a merchant, who delivered it to Liangzhou.
The Venerable Buddhavarman—Buddhavarman (translated into Chinese as Juexian)—was of the Śākya clan and a native of Kapilavastu. He was a descendant of King Amṛtodana.
Having lost both parents in childhood, he left the household life as a śrāmaṇera. At the age of sixteen, he had extensively studied the various...
The Sūtra-master was profoundly versed in dhyāna and the Vinaya. He once traveled with Saṃghadatta to Kaśmīra.
While Saṃghadatta sat in meditation with his door closed, he suddenly saw the Master arrive and say, "I am going briefly to Tuṣita Heaven to pay my respects to Maitreya. Having spoken, he vanished.

Later, witnessing even more of his supernatural transformations, [the Master] prayed to him with reverence and inquired, only then learning that he had attained the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin). At that time, the Śramaṇa Zhi... of the Yao Qin dynasty... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
When Guṇavarman arrived in Kaśmīra, he beheld the purity of the monastic community and, sighing with regret as he gazed toward the east, said:

"My fellow practitioners have not yet encountered a true master; by what means shall they attain awakening? He then consulted the assembly, asking: "Who is capable of fulfilling my request to spread the teachings in the eastern lands?
They all responded in unison: "Guṇabhadra is the man for this. Guṇavarman then entreated the Master to pack his provisions and set out on the journey. After traveling...
Traveling through various countries, he reached Jiaozhi, where he boarded a merchant vessel and followed the coast until he arrived at Donglai in Qingzhou.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an, he immediately went there to follow him. Prince Hong of the Qin invited the Master to the Eastern Palace to assemble the multitude and preach the Dharma.
There, he debated the meaning of form and emptiness with Kumārajīva. The Master said: "You have only been able to explain the form and emptiness of the fruit; you have not explained..."

He attained the realization that form is empty within its causes. Kumārajīva asked what this meant. The Master said: "Because a single atom is empty, the collection of atoms is empty; because the collection of atoms is empty, a single atom is empty.
Within the emptiness of a single atom there is no collection of atoms; within the emptiness of the collection of atoms there is no single atom.

After several rounds of such exchange, Kumārajīva could not fathom it. Emperor Yao Xing of Qin provided support for three thousand monks and grandly performed the rites of hospitality, yet the Master—
Practicing meditation in quietude and maintaining his self-restraint, he suddenly said to his disciples:
"I have seen five ships depart from my native land together. The multitude called this a false claim and consequently banished me.

Thereupon, accompanied by over forty disciples, including Huìyán and Huìguān, he set out for Mount Lú and took up residence in a thatched hut at Xiānggǔ (the *líng* [pronounced *pó*] grass hut). At that time, Master Hóngyuǎn of the Lotus Society heard that the Master had been...

The expulsion was based on a record kept by his disciples; according to the Vinaya, there was no offense. He immediately dispatched his disciple Tanyong to deliver a letter to the Ruler of Qin to request his reinstatement from the expulsion.
Thereupon, he invited the Master to Donglin Temple to translate various sutras on Dhyāna and Abhidharma.

From that time on, those in Jiangdong began to take delight in the joy of meditation. The Master’s aspiration lay in traveling to convert others, so he went west to Jiangling, where he carried his alms bowl for the practice of *piṇḍapāta*. Indeed...
He saw five ships from India arrive. Subsequently, he returned to the capital and established Daochang Monastery.
Previously, Zhi Falin had obtained the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in thirty-six thousand stanzas at Khotan, which had not yet been translated.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Meng Yi, the Prefect of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, requested that the Master serve as the chief translator. Together with...
The śramaṇas Fayè, Huiyì, Huìyán, Huìguān, and others served as scribes for the translation, which comprised sixty fascicles.
There were two youths in blue robes who emerged from the pond to sprinkle water, sweep, and grind ink.

As the Master translated them successively, there were the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, the *Pratipattisādhanaśāstra*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* obtained by Faxian. Altogether...
Fifteen sections. In the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while recollecting the Buddha. His stupa was erected on the northern ridge of Mount Lu.
Liu Chengzhi—whose courtesy name was Zhongsī—was a native of Pengcheng and a descendant of Liu An, the Prince Yuan of Han. He was profoundly skilled in the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*, and furthermore...

He was well-versed in the works of the hundred schools of thought. Having lost his father at a young age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned. Confident in his own talent, he did not involve himself in worldly affairs.

When he first donned the official robes, he was appointed as a military aide (*chamjun*) to a provincial governor. Xie An and Liu Yu, admiring his virtue, both recommended him for office, yet he declined their offers with all his might.

By nature, he was fond of Buddhist principles; he therefore went to Mount Lu and devoted himself entirely to the master Huiyuan. Huiyuan said to him, "Your official rank is lofty and eminent; what do you wish to do?"

[The questioner] asked: "Why did you do this? He replied: "The ruler and his ministers were suspicious of one another; why would I involve myself in such matters? Because Liu Yu could not bend him, he honored him with the title "Yimin" (Remnant of the People).
When Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zong Bing, Zhang Quan, Bi Yingzhi, and others arrived at Mount Lu together, Master Huiyuan said to them:
"Now that you gentlemen have come here, should you not also consider embarking on the journey to the Pure Land? Cheng [continued].
He then incised the rock to create a text of his vow to commemorate the event (the text appears in the *Lushan ji*).

Subsequently, he established a separate meditation hall north of the West Grove Stream (*Xilin*), where he cultivated his aspirations amidst poverty, meticulously investigating profound principles while concurrently observing the prohibitive precepts. Hui-zong, Hui-zhang, and others all marveled at and revered him.
He once sent a letter to Guanzhong to discuss the meaning of the scriptures with Kumārajīva and Sengzhao, and he composed the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).

The poem expresses his intent to focus single-mindedly on seated meditation. Within half a year, while in a state of meditative concentration, he saw Buddha-light illuminating the ground, all of which turned the color of gold.
After fifteen years, while in the midst of right mindfulness of the Buddha, he beheld Amitābha Buddha.
The light from his jade-white brow shone forth; he lowered his hand to comfort and receive him. Cheng said, "How might the Tathāgata rub the crown of my head and cover me with his robe?
Suddenly, the Buddha rubbed his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him.

On another day, as he was recollecting the Buddha, he again saw himself entering a pool of seven treasures, where the lotuses were blue and white and the water was deep and clear. There was a person whose head was encircled by a halo, and from whose chest [light] issued forth.

Pointing to the water in the pond with his hand marked by the *svastika* (the sound of which is "wan," signifying the Buddha's possession of the ten thousand virtues), he said: "This is water of eight meritorious qualities; you may drink from it."
Chengzhi found the water he drank to be sweet and delicious; even upon waking, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores.
He then comforted himself, saying, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived. He further requested monks to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* nearly several hundred times.
Later, when the monks from Mount Lu had all assembled, Chengzhi burned incense before the images, prostrated twice, and made this vow: "By means of the Buddha Śākyamuni..."
Because of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, one knows that there is Amitābha Buddha.
This incense should first be offered to Tathāgata Śākyamuni, next to Amitābha Buddha, and furthermore to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is by virtue of this sūtra that one attains birth in the Pure Land. By the merit of this sūtra, may all sentient beings together be born in the Pure Land. Thus, he [bestowed it].
The assembly lay separately upon their beds; facing west with palms joined, he passed away. He instructed his son Yong to pile up earth to form a tomb and not to use a coffin or outer casing.
This was during the sixth year of the Yixi era. He was fifty-nine years of age (the *Lushan ji* records the details of his miraculous responses in great detail).

Zhang Ye, whose courtesy name was Laimin, resided at Zisang in Xunyang. He was related by marriage to Yuanming (Tao Qian). Zhang Ye’s learning encompassed both Chinese and Buddhist traditions, and he was particularly skilled in literary composition.
By nature, he was filial and fraternal; he gave away all his fields and houses to his younger brother, sharing even the sweetest flavors with him.
